description: We are a team of passionate students and we want to make an example of how capable a team of great people can be, no matter the age. Our team's name is inspired by the American astronomer Carl Saegan, who inspires us every day.
summary:
PROJECT R.E.D. (Resilient Extraterrestrial Dwelling)

What we developed: A 5-turn tactical simulator where players manage a Martian habitat by strategically investing limited technology across five core life-support systems (Energy, Air, Water, Food, and Protection) while keeping crew morale high. Guided by an AI robot named Marquitos, players navigate random environmental hazards—such as dust storms and solar flares—through interactive minigames and critical resource trade-offs.

PROJECT R.E.D. makes real-world aerospace engineering trade-offs tangible and fun rather than overly simplified or overwhelming. Every mechanic is grounded in real space science, integrating NASA/CSA data on MOXIE oxygen extraction, 98% ISS water recycling, regolith perchlorate toxicity, DONKI space weather alerts, and OSDR biological research.

It bridges complex space science and STEM education, empowering young learners to experience firsthand how interconnected decisions, resource management, and emergency responses dictate whether a mission succeeds or fails.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

PROJECT R.E.D. (Resilient Extraterrestrial Dwelling) is a 2D isometric turn-based management game where players take on the role of mission commander for an advanced human outpost on Mars.

  • Pre-Mission Configuration: Before landing, players allocate limited technology across five primary life-support systems (Energy, Air, Water, Food, and Protection), choosing to upgrade only two systems to maximum technology while leaving three at a baseline generic level.
  • Five-Turn Crisis Deck: Over five operational turns, the base encounters random environmental and internal emergencies drawn from an event deck (such as global dust storms, solar flares, CO₂ alarms, clogged water recyclers, or food mold).
  • Interactive Minigames: Emergencies trigger fast-paced minigames (balancing pressure bars, button sequences, or connecting wire circuits) to resolve active hazards.
  • Daily Nutrition & Morale: Players select three meals daily from a 9-item space menu (rehydratable, thermo-stabilized, and long-shelf-life items) to balance astronaut nutrition and maintain a hidden sixth system: Crew Morale.
  • AI Companion "Marquitos": An assistant robot accompanies the player, delivering real NASA/CSA space trivia, Earth updates, and post-mission evaluations.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

The project bridges complex aerospace engineering and STEM education for youth and students. By replacing abstract formulas with tangible choices, it demonstrates that extraterrestrial survival is not a game of luck, but a series of interconnected engineering decisions. Students gain a realistic understanding of resource scarcity, environmental hazards, and the vital role of space research, inspiring the next generation of space scientists, engineers, and astronauts.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

  • Game Engine & Scripting: Godot Engine 4.7 (GDScript) for state management, turn logic, minigames, and 2D isometric rendering.
  • Graphics & Design: Custom pixel-art sprites for 12 habitat modules, 9 space food items, atmospheric storm overlays, and character animations for the robot Marquitos.
  • Scientific Data Sources: NASA Technical Reports (nominal life-support references), NASA OSDR (biological impacts of spaceflight: OSD-1010, OSD-984, OSD-977, OSD-815, OSD-767), NASA CCMC DONKI (real-time space weather tracking), and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) educational toolkits.

How is the project creative?

PROJECT R.E.D. transforms rigorous scientific data into an intuitive, gamified experience.

  • Translating Metrics into Mechanics: Real parameters—such as MOXIE requiring 798 °C to split CO₂, ISS water recovery increasing from 93% to 98% via brine processors, or surface radiation reaching 0.64 mSv/day—are translated into balanced resource trade-offs rather than overwhelming spreadsheets.
  • Educational Continuity ("What Would Have Happened"): At the end of the mission, Marquitos reads a review explaining the outcome of unchosen event cards, ensuring players learn from every scenario—even those they didn't encounter during gameplay.

What factors were considered?

  • System Interdependence: Energy powers MOXIE and greenhouse LEDs; water is required for electrolysis and meal rehydration; soil perchlorates (0.4%–1%) mandate hydroponics over direct planting.
  • Real-World Constraints: We factored in real space exploration challenges like planet-encircling dust storms, communication delays of 4 to 24 minutes, and long-term vitamin degradation (C, B1, B9) in packaged space food.
